peak.shareBasis: common shares; adjusted for 2-for-1 splits in 1985 and 1986 and 5-for-4 splits in Dec 1996 and Jun 1997 (none after)

peakLine: $1,000 at the peak (Jun 2021) was worth $0 by Oct 2025
epitaph: 1,392 stores in Feb 2024. Filed 9 Sep 2024.
seoTitle: Big Lots bankruptcy: what happened (9 Sep 2024)
keyFacts: Big Lots was a home discount retailer based in Columbus, Ohio.
In Feb 2024 it ran 1,392 stores in 48 states and had about 30,300 active associates.
It filed for Chapter 11 on Sept 9, 2024, citing inflation and high interest rates, and planned to sell itself to private equity firm Nexus Capital Management.
It later sold its stores, distribution centers and brand to Gordon Brothers instead, in a sale that closed on Jan 3, 2025.
In Oct 2025 it asked to convert to Chapter 7 liquidation and said its common shares were worthless.

name: Tupperware

peak.shareBasis: common shares; no splits since the 1996 listing

peakLine: $1,000 at the peak (Dec 2013) was worth $0 by Jun 2025
epitaph: Airtight seal since 1946. Filed 17 Sep 2024.
seoTitle: Tupperware bankruptcy: what happened (17 Sep 2024)
keyFacts: Tupperware's roots date to 1946, when chemist Earl Tupper set out to make a plastic container with an airtight seal.
The first Tupperware parties were held in 1948 and became its main way of selling.
Tupperware became a separate public company on May 31, 1996, when Premark International spun it off to its shareholders.
Its shares peaked in late 2013, reaching a high of $97.14 in the fourth quarter.
Sales had been in steady decline since 2018 as competition rose.
At its Sept 2024 filing it reported more than $1.2 billion in debts and $679.5 million in assets, and had more than 5,450 employees in 41 countries.
Companies formed by its lenders bought the Tupperware business in a sale that closed on Nov 27, 2024.
The court confirmed a liquidation plan in May 2025 that gave shareholders nothing and cancelled their shares.

name: Nikola

peak.shareBasis: post-June 2024 1-for-30 reverse split shares ($79.73 per share as traded in June 2020, times 30)

peakLine: $1,000 at the peak (Jun 2020) was worth $0 by Dec 2025
epitaph: Worth more than Ford in Jun 2020. Filed Feb 2025.
seoTitle: Nikola bankruptcy: what happened (19 Feb 2025)
keyFacts: Nikola began trading on Nasdaq on June 4, 2020, after merging with the blank-check company VectoIQ.
Based on its June 9, 2020 closing price of $79.73, Nikola was valued at about $28.8 billion, slightly more than Ford.
Founder Trevor Milton was convicted of securities fraud and wire fraud in Oct 2022 and sentenced to four years in prison in Dec 2023.
Prosecutors said Nikola's retail investors lost more than $660 million.
It did a 1-for-30 reverse stock split in June 2024.
It filed for Chapter 11 on Feb 19, 2025 with about $47 million in cash, planning to sell its assets.
In April 2025 Lucid Group bought some of its assets for $10 million, plus $7 million more under set conditions.
The court confirmed a liquidation plan in Sept 2025 that cancelled all Nikola shares for no value.

back.what: New GM listed on the NYSE in an IPO priced at $33 a share

peak.shareBasis: old GM common stock (NYSE: GM); no splits between 2000 and 2009

peakLine: $1,000 at the peak (Apr 2000) was worth $0 by Mar 2011
epitaph: Filed Jun 2009. Back on the NYSE Nov 2010.
seoTitle: General Motors bankruptcy and comeback: what happened (1 Jun 2009)
keyFacts: GM stock closed at a peak of $93.63 on April 28, 2000.
On May 29, 2009, the stock closed at 75 cents, its lowest level since the Great Depression.
GM filed for bankruptcy on June 1, 2009, and the US Treasury provided a $30.1 billion debtor-in-possession loan.
The new GM company emerged from bankruptcy 40 days after the filing.
Old GM became Motors Liquidation Company, and its stock was cancelled on March 31, 2011.
New GM raised $20.1 billion in its IPO on November 18, 2010, at $33 a share.
The IPO cut the Treasury's stake in GM from about 61 percent to 33 percent.

name: Marvel Entertainment Group

back.what: Merged with Toy Biz, which renamed itself Marvel Enterprises; its common stock traded on the NYSE

epitaph: Every hero needs an origin story. Filed 1996.
seoTitle: Marvel bankruptcy and comeback: what happened (27 Dec 1996)
keyFacts: Marvel Entertainment Group was the largest US comic book publisher and the top maker of trading cards when it filed for Chapter 11 on December 27, 1996.
Its stock was sold to the public in 1991 and, adjusted for splits, climbed past $34 about two and a half years later.
The stock closed at $2.375 on December 26, 1996, and NYSE trading was halted after the bankruptcy news.
In its filing, Marvel listed assets of $229.6 million and liabilities of $693.2 million.
Ronald Perelman owned about 81 percent of Marvel at the time of the filing.
On October 1, 1998, Marvel merged with Toy Biz, which changed its name to Marvel Enterprises.

seoTitle: Six Flags bankruptcy and comeback: what happened (13 Jun 2009)
keyFacts: Six Flags filed for Chapter 11 on June 13, 2009, in Delaware, while carrying about $2.4 billion in debt.
The company said all 20 of its North American parks would stay open during the bankruptcy.
The NYSE delisted the stock on April 17, 2009, when its last NYSE trade was 13 cents.
Chairman Daniel Snyder owned about 6 percent of the shares at the time of the filing.
Six Flags left bankruptcy on April 30, 2010, and changed its name to Six Flags Entertainment Corporation.
The NYSE listed the new company's shares on June 21, 2010, under the old symbol SIX.

name: Hertz

back.what: Reorganized Hertz Global's new stock began trading on Nasdaq under HTZ

epitaph: Rare: old shareholders got paid. Back 2021.
seoTitle: Hertz bankruptcy and comeback: what happened (22 May 2020)
keyFacts: Hertz traces its vehicle rental business back to 1918.
Hertz filed for Chapter 11 on May 22, 2020, after rental demand collapsed during pandemic lockdowns.
The NYSE suspended trading in the stock after October 29, 2020, and it moved to the over-the-counter market as HTZGQ.
The winning bid from Knighthead Capital and Certares in May 2021 included a rare payout to existing shareholders.
Old shareholders received $1.53 in cash per share plus a small stake in the new company and warrants or rights.
Hertz left bankruptcy on June 30, 2021.
On November 9, 2021, its new stock began trading on Nasdaq and closed its first day at $26.17.

name: Delta Air Lines

back.what: New Delta common stock was listed on the NYSE and began trading under DAL

peak.shareBasis: shares after the November 1998 two-for-one split (old NYSE: DAL); highest quarterly closing price, quarter ended June 30, 1999

peakLine: $1,000 at the peak (1999) was worth $0 by Apr 2007
epitaph: Filed same day as Northwest, 2005. Back 2007.
seoTitle: Delta Air Lines bankruptcy and comeback: what happened (14 Sep 2005)
keyFacts: Delta filed for Chapter 11 on September 14, 2005, the same day as Northwest Airlines.
High fuel costs, heavy debt and pension obligations drove the filing.
Delta listed $21.6 billion in assets, which made it one of the ten largest US bankruptcies by assets at the time.
Delta had lost nearly $10 billion over the four years before the filing.
The NYSE suspended Delta stock on October 13, 2005, and it then traded on the Pink Sheets as DALRQ.
When Delta left bankruptcy on April 30, 2007, the old stock was cancelled and new shares went to creditors, including pilots, and to about 39,000 employees.
The new Delta stock began trading on the NYSE on May 3, 2007.

name: Kmart

back.what: Stock of the new Kmart Holding Corporation began trading on the Nasdaq National Market under KMRT, after trading on the OTC Bulletin Board

epitaph: Filed Jan 2002. Back on Nasdaq Jun 2003.
seoTitle: Kmart bankruptcy and comeback: what happened (22 Jan 2002)
keyFacts: Kmart grew out of the business S.S. Kresge started with his first store in 1899; the first Kmart store opened in March 1962.
At the time of its filing, Kmart ran more than 2,100 stores with about 240,000 employees and had yearly sales of about $37 billion.
Kmart filed for Chapter 11 in Chicago on January 22, 2002, after its sole grocery supplier stopped shipments.
Kmart stock closed at $4.74 on January 2, 2002, and at $1.74 on January 18, the last trading day before the filing.
The NYSE suspended trading in the old Kmart stock on December 19, 2002.
Kmart left bankruptcy on May 6, 2003, as a unit of the new Kmart Holding Corporation, with ESL Investments and Third Avenue as plan investors.
The new stock began trading on Nasdaq on June 10, 2003, under the symbol KMRT.

name: AMR Corporation (American Airlines)

back.what: AMR merged with US Airways to form American Airlines Group, whose stock began trading on Nasdaq under AAL

peak.shareBasis: AMR shares after the June 1998 two-for-one split; highest quarterly closing price, quarter ended Sept 30, 1998; not adjusted for the March 2000 Sabre share distribution

epitaph: Filed 2011. Landed in a merger, Dec 2013.
seoTitle: American Airlines (AMR) bankruptcy and comeback: what happened (29 Nov 2011)
keyFacts: AMR, the parent of American Airlines, filed for Chapter 11 in New York on November 29, 2011, to get a cost and debt structure it called industry competitive.
American Airlines kept flying its normal schedule during the bankruptcy.
The NYSE suspended AMR stock on January 5, 2012, and it then traded over the counter as AAMRQ.
In an unusual turn, the merger deal with US Airways gave AMR shareholders 3.5 percent of the new company, and more if its share price rose.
AMR merged with US Airways on December 9, 2013, forming American Airlines Group, then the world's largest airline by passenger miles.
By April 8, 2014, each old AMR share had brought 0.744 shares of the new company, worth $26.77 that day.
Old AMR holders ended up with about a third of the merged company's stock.

name: PG&E

back.what: PG&E emerged from Chapter 11; its stock had kept trading on the NYSE throughout

peak.shareBasis: PG&E Corporation common stock (NYSE: PCG); no splits

peakLine: $1,000 at the peak (Sep 2017) was worth $126 by Jul 2020
epitaph: Filed Jan 2019. Kept trading all the way through.
seoTitle: PG&E bankruptcy and comeback: what happened (29 Jan 2019)
keyFacts: PG&E serves about 16 million customers in Northern and central California.
In January 2019, PG&E said it faced up to $30 billion in potential liability over its role in California wildfires.
Fire investigators blamed the utility's power lines for a number of wildfires in 2017 and 2018.
PG&E filed for Chapter 11 on January 29, 2019.
In December 2019, PG&E announced a $13.5 billion settlement of claims tied to several wildfires, including the 2018 Camp Fire.
PG&E left bankruptcy on July 1, 2020, and its existing shareholders kept much of the company.
Under the plan, a trust for fire victims was to own 22.19 percent of PG&E's stock.

name: UAL Corporation (United Airlines)

back.what: New UAL common stock was listed on the Nasdaq National Market and began trading under UAUA

peak.shareBasis: UAL common stock after the May 1996 four-for-one split; highest quarterly sales price, fourth quarter of 1997

peakLine: $1,000 at the peak (1997) was worth $0 by Feb 2006
epitaph: 1,150 days in Chapter 11. Back on Nasdaq 2006.
seoTitle: United Airlines (UAL) bankruptcy and comeback: what happened (9 Dec 2002)
keyFacts: UAL, parent of United Airlines, filed for Chapter 11 in Chicago on December 9, 2002, days after the US government rejected its bid for federal loan guarantees.
UAL listed $22.8 billion in assets and $21.2 billion in liabilities, the largest bankruptcy in aviation history at the time.
Employees owned 55 percent of the carrier under a 1994 plan.
United had cut service and laid off nearly 20,000 workers after the September 11 attacks.
The old stock traded over the counter as UALAQ from April 2003 until February 2006.
United left bankruptcy on February 1, 2006, after 1,150 days, the longest and costliest airline restructuring up to then.
The new UAL stock began trading on Nasdaq on February 2, 2006.

name: Texaco

back.what: Texaco left Chapter 11 after paying Pennzoil a $3 billion cash settlement; the bankruptcy court issued its notice of plan confirmation and discharge that day, and the stock had stayed on the NYSE throughout

epitaph: Biggest filing yet, 1987. Out within a year.
seoTitle: Texaco bankruptcy and comeback: what happened (12 Apr 1987)
keyFacts: In 1985 a Texas jury found that Texaco had interfered with Pennzoil's agreement to buy Getty Oil and awarded Pennzoil $10.53 billion.
Texaco, then the eighth-largest US company with $34 billion in assets, filed for Chapter 11 on April 12, 1987, the biggest bankruptcy filing up to that time.
Texaco said the only reason for the filing was to keep the Pennzoil judgment from crippling the company, and it kept running its business.
Texaco stock fell $3 a share in early trading on the first day after the filing.
During the case, Texaco and Pennzoil settled for $3 billion in cash, and the court approved the deal in December 1987.
The court confirmed Texaco's reorganization plan on March 23, 1988, and issued its notice of confirmation and discharge on April 7, 1988.
